Let <MATH_0001> be a morphism of algebraic stacks.
<STRUCT_0001>
<STRUCT_0002> We say <MATH_0002> is <TEXTITOPEN_0001>DM<TEXTITCLOSE_0001> if <MATH_0003> is unramified<FOOTNOTEOPEN_0001>The
letters DM stand for Deligne-Mumford. If <MATH_0004> is DM then given any scheme
<MATH_0005> and any morphism <MATH_0006> the fibre product
<MATH_0007>
is an algebraic stack over <MATH_0008> whose diagonal is unramified, i.e.,
<MATH_0009> is DM. This implies <MATH_0010>
is a Deligne-Mumford stack, see Theorem <REF_0001>.
In other words a DM morphism is one whose ``fibres'' are Deligne-Mumford
stacks. This hopefully at least motivates the terminology.<FOOTNOTECLOSE_0001>.
<STRUCT_0003> We say <MATH_0011> is <TEXTITOPEN_0002>quasi-DM<TEXTITCLOSE_0002> if <MATH_0012> is
locally quasi-finite<FOOTNOTEOPEN_0002>If <MATH_0013> is quasi-DM, then the
``fibres'' <MATH_0014> of <MATH_0015> are quasi-DM. An
algebraic stack <MATH_0016> is quasi-DM exactly if there exists a
scheme <MATH_0017> and a surjective flat morphism <MATH_0018> of finite
presentation which is locally quasi-finite, see
Theorem <REF_0002>.
Note the similarity to being Deligne-Mumford, which
is defined in terms of having an <ACCENT_0001>tale covering by a scheme.<FOOTNOTECLOSE_0002>.
<STRUCT_0004> We say <MATH_0019> is <TEXTITOPEN_0003>separated<TEXTITCLOSE_0003> if <MATH_0020> is proper.
<STRUCT_0005> We say <MATH_0021> is <TEXTITOPEN_0004>quasi-separated<TEXTITCLOSE_0004> if <MATH_0022>
is quasi-compact and quasi-separated.
<STRUCT_0006>

<STRUCT_0001>
In this definition we are using that <MATH_0001> is representable by algebraic
spaces and we are using
Properties of Stacks,
Section <REF_0001>
to make sense out of imposing conditions on <MATH_0002>.
We note that these definitions do not conflict with the already
existing notions if <MATH_0003> is representable by algebraic spaces, see
Lemmas <REF_0002> and
<REF_0003>.
There is an interesting way to characterize these conditions by looking
at higher diagonals, see
Lemma <REF_0004>.
